newsitem.title: USA: CFTC to decide on speedy contract approval in Feb.
newsitem.headline: CFTC to decide on speedy contract approval in Feb.

text.p: Commodity Futures Trading Commission will make a final decision by the end of February on its proposal to speed up the approval process for new futures contracts, the commission's chairwoman said Wednesday.
The commission received a variety of comments on a preliminary proposal issued in November that would create a "fast-track" process allowing some new contracts to be approved in as few as 10 days.
CFTC staff is reviewing the comments and the commission will "decide by the end of February whether to adopt it in the original form," chairwoman Brooksley Born said.
The commission could also decide to alter or withdraw the preliminary proposal, which was criticized as inadequate by some of the large futures exchanges.

Congress is also expected to take up the issue. A bill introduced in the Senate last year that would have speeded up the process for most contracts will be reintroduced soon, legislators have said. CFTC officials said last year's bill might not give them enough time to review new contract proposals.
Speaking to reporters after a speech to the D.C. Bar here, Born said the commission was still in deliberations.
"Ten days doesn't seem very long to me," she said in answer to a question about whether the commission would consider shortening the time schedule set out on the November proposal.

Asked if she would consider shortening the schedule for contracts that did not qualify for the 10 day "fast track" process, Born said the commission staff is looking at all comment letters and conducting an "in depth" review.
"I'm committed to streamlining our procedures where the staff feels that we can do so," she said.
Born also told reporters she expected the commission would complete a report on the adequacy of exchange audit trails in the next several months.

The commission is also analyzing comments criticizing a proposal governing statements by commodity advisers on the Internet, Born said. The commission backed off an initial proposal issued last year, she noted.

The commission is continuing to discuss with the Treasury Department proposals to amend or clarify a controversial 1974 amendment to the Comodity Exchange Act known as the Treasury Amendment, Born said.
The two agencies have been attempting to hash out a compromise for many months without success.

Federal courts have given conflicting interpretations to the amendment, which was designed to free banks from CFTC oversight when trading in foreign exchange and certain other markets. Congress asked the two agencies to craft a proposal to eliminate the ambiguity by the end of 1996, but "we haven't done so yet," Born said.
Born said an increase in the number of closed sessions at the CFTC during her first five months as chairwoman was simply to resolve a backlog of 48 enforcement cases pending when she took office.
Born declined to comment on the commission's ongoing investigation of wrongdoing in the copper market in the wake of a $2 billion loss by Sumitomo Corp.
